r3-p01-000: Low-Cost Bridge Vibration Anomaly Detection System Robust to Temperature and Humidity
r3-p01-002: Sudden collapses of aging bridges — a recurring social problem
r3-p01-003: In April 2023, the walkway of the roughly 30-year-old Jeongja Bridge in Bundang collapsed during ordinary pedestrian use after corrosion and damage accumulated in its cantilever members, killing one person and injuring another. In July 2026, a roughly 50 m section of Boritdol Bridge, an over-sea footbridge in Guryongpo, Pohang, fell into the sea — even though it had received a C grade in a recent inspection and had been repaired and reinforced the previous year; accumulated fatigue from wave action is among the suspected causes. In both cases the bridge collapsed before the next inspection even after warning signs had been observed or repairs made, showing that periodic inspection alone cannot track changes in structural condition continuously enough to prevent accidents.
r3-p01-006: As in these two cases, the corrosion, cracking and fatigue that accumulate over years in aging bridges change dynamic properties such as stiffness, damping and natural frequency, so they can be observed through vibration-based monitoring. Vibration characteristics, however, change not only with damage but also with environmental variables such as temperature and humidity, making it hard to tell whether an observed change comes from damage or from the environment. Two tasks remain: capturing changes in dynamic properties continuously between inspections, and separating the environmental effect from those changes so that only damage-related anomalies are flagged.
r3-p01-007: According to the Korea Authority of Land & Infrastructure Safety's 2025 statistics by facility class (classified by size), Korea has 37,543 bridges — 5,392 Class 1, 7,925 Class 2 and 24,226 Class 3 — and the relatively small Class 3 bridges account for about 64.5%. Because so many structures must be managed, the need for low-cost, continuous screening that also works on small and medium-sized bridges keeps growing.

r3-p01-009: The continuous-monitoring blind spot of small and medium bridges
r3-p01-010: Independently of its size, a bridge's condition is rated by safety grade (A–E), and statutory inspections are divided into the precision safety inspection, which checks and evaluates a facility's current condition, and the precision safety diagnosis, a deeper stage that verifies structural safety through engineering analysis and even evaluates load-carrying capacity (Fig. 4). From December 2025, precision safety diagnosis was
r3-p02-000: extended to aging and low-grade (C·D·E) facilities as well. Precision safety diagnosis, however, is costly and labor-intensive and is performed only on a fixed cycle — every 4 to 6 years depending on the safety grade — so a time gap remains between inspections, and changes in dynamic properties that accumulate during that gap are hard to detect. As a result, aging small and medium bridges such as pedestrian overpasses and small footbridges lack a low-cost supplementary means of continuously detecting changes in condition between inspections.

r3-p02-002: No low-cost screening technology before precision diagnosis
r3-p02-003: Existing SHM (Structural Health Monitoring) systems install sensors on a structure permanently for continuous measurement, but they rely on precision equipment and dedicated infrastructure — ultra-precise piezoelectric accelerometers, high-performance data-acquisition hardware, distributed fiber-optic sensors (e.g., KRISS BOCDA) — and are therefore applied mainly to a few large, critical bridges such as Incheon Bridge; their cost and installation constraints make them impractical to deploy widely on small and medium aging bridges in service. Between periodic precision diagnosis and costly continuous measurement, low-cost continuous screening that precedes precision diagnosis is effectively missing. Bridge safety management therefore needs a multi-stage concept in which continuous screening (stage-1 triage) filters out anomaly candidates before precision safety inspection and diagnosis, so that limited inspection staff and budgets can be concentrated on suspect bridges.
r3-p02-005: This work addresses the three problems summarized above: ① capturing changes in dynamic properties continuously between inspections while separating environmental effects, ② the time gap between precision-diagnosis cycles, and ③ the difficulty of applying precision measurement systems to small and medium aging bridges. It is not a system that predicts collapse or replaces precision safety diagnosis; it is a low-cost stage-1 (supplementary) screening system that fills the time gap between inspections and diagnoses by indicating which bridges should be inspected first.
r3-p02-006: The purpose of this work is to develop a low-cost, machine-learning-based bridge vibration screening system that addresses this blind spot and this missing technology at the same time, with three goals. First, vibration data are collected with an ADXL355Z MEMS accelerometer and a Raspberry Pi (3 Model A+ in stage 1, 5 in stage 2); because damage data cannot be created deliberately on a bridge in service, unsupervised learning trained only on normal data is used. Second, since a bridge's natural frequency rises and falls with air temperature and humidity even without damage [2], DHT22 and DS18B20 sensors record air temperature, surface temperature and relative humidity, and the normal temperature/humidity–natural-frequency relationship is learned so that variation explained by the environment is removed and false alarms are reduced. Third, because an anomaly signal alone does not tell an inspector where to look, the system implements explainable alarms that also show which frequency bands deviated from the normal baseline, guiding the direction of the follow-up precision inspection.
r3-p02-008: The three goals are implemented as a single unsupervised anomaly-detection pipeline. 1) Only the vibration patterns of the normal state are learned; 2) after normal variation explained by temperature and humidity is removed first, a residual that deviates strongly from the learned pattern is judged an anomaly candidate; and 3) the system visualizes which frequency bands have a large reconstruction error (the difference between the input and its reconstruction from the learned normal pattern, which grows as the input departs from normal — see 2.3), providing interpretive information that supports the choice of inspection direction rather than a definitive diagnosis. The hardware is described in 2.2, and the concrete procedure that links the three functions is covered step by step in 2.3 Operating Principle.
r3-p03-001: SHM systems based on low-cost MEMS accelerometers
r3-p03-002: An SHM study combined a Raspberry Pi with a low-cost MEMS accelerometer (ADXL355Z) and showed that a structure's natural frequencies, mode shapes and damping can be identified without ultra-precise piezoelectric sensors costing tens of millions of won [1]. That study, however, focuses on identifying dynamic characteristics and does not address how environmental variables such as temperature and humidity, or changes in operational loading, affect anomaly detection.
r3-p03-004: The BOCDA-based fiber-optic sensor system of the Korea Research Institute of Standards and Science (KRISS) precisely measures strain and load position in a structure with high spatial resolution [4]. As precision strain measurement that presupposes dedicated infrastructure, it differs from this work's vibration-based continuous screening in both the physical quantity measured and its purpose.
r3-p03-006: The Swiss Z24 Bridge Benchmark (provided by KU Leuven) is a representative public dataset that includes long-term monitoring and progressive damage-test data [3]. Many unsupervised models — Autoencoder, One-Class SVM, Isolation Forest, VAE and others — have been compared on Z24 [5][6], but most stop at outputting an anomaly score or a threshold exceedance and do not explain which band departed from the baseline.
r3-p03-007: Environmental-compensation research on long-term data from a full-scale bridge
r3-p03-008: The openLAB Research Bridge public dataset, from the long-term monitoring of a full-scale research bridge in Bautzen, Germany, provides acceleration responses together with environmental measurements such as air temperature and humidity, making it well suited to analyzing seasonal and daily temperature effects (details in 2.7) [8]. In this work, openLAB serves as supplementary validation data for checking whether the environmental-compensation principle also holds on full-scale long-term data; the core contribution lies in a low-cost hardware implementation that links collection, compensation, judgment and explanation in one pipeline, and in validation with our own model bridges, which distinguishes it from studies that reanalyze public data.
r3-p03-009: The distinctiveness of this work therefore rests on three axes: direct low-cost hardware implementation, temperature/humidity compensation, and band-wise explainability. Unlike low-cost MEMS studies, it reduces false alarms through temperature/humidity compensation; unlike fiber-optic measurement, it performs continuous screening with inexpensive general-purpose parts; and unlike unsupervised studies that output only an anomaly score, it also reports the contribution of each band to the reconstruction error.
r3-p03-011: This system is a supplementary vibration-screening system that collects vibration, temperature and relative humidity with a low-cost MEMS accelerometer (ADXL355Z) and a temperature/humidity sensor (DHT22), reduces environment-driven false alarms using the temperature/humidity–frequency relationship learned in the normal state, detects anomaly candidates that depart from the normal pattern with an Autoencoder, and reports them together with the frequency bands that have large reconstruction errors. Our own experiments proceed in three stages. Stage 1 confirms that the whole collection–compensation–detection–explanation pipeline works, using a foam-board model and manual excitation. Stage 2 overcomes stage 1's two limitations (indistinct resonance peaks and variation in manual excitation) with an aluminum multi-span model and a solenoid auto-tapper, validates discrimination performance on a matrix of temperature, humidity, mass and bolt-loosening conditions, and builds a real-time measurement and analysis setup based on a Raspberry Pi 5. Stage 3 moves the system to two real pedestrian overpasses to examine environmental effects and detection power (details in 2.2 and 3.1).
